extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians and advanced students (readers of a 19th-century mathematical journal)
extracted.subtask_description: Short research/expository papers on geometry, numerical methods, and integral reduction (examples include demonstrations of Pascal/Brianchon, algorithms for computing logarithms/antilogarithms, and reduction of integrals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of logarithm/antilogarithm tables (Tables I–IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables I and II consist of the modulus (M) and of the reciprocal of the modulus, together with their multiples as far as 9. Table III contains Napierian and common logarithms of selected integers; Table IV gives logarithms of reciprocals (not of the numbers in the first column but of their reciprocals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute logs of 2, 3, 5, 7 by known methods; derive reciprocal of the modulus and the logarithms in Table III by addition/subtraction. Arrange numbers of Table IV in nine horizontal rows (1−0.01, 1−0.001, etc.); use formula (a) (series expansion with A, B, C coefficients) to compute the Napierian logs of reciprocals; then obtain common logs by multiplying by the modulus M or by independent calculation using A·M, B·M, etc. Explains that A, B, C are independent of m so remaining entries in a row follow by simple shifts and additions, easing table construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm to compute log(N) to p decimal places
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce N to a number between 1 and 2 by moving the decimal and dividing by an initial digit b so the integral part becomes 1; denote quotient 1 + w. Repeatedly divide the fractional part by 1 + w_i producing one-significant-figure quotients r1, r2, … until remainder w_m begins with at least p ciphers. Use product relations and logarithms of factors to build log(N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key identity: log(1 + w) = sum_j [log(1/(1−r_j))] + log(1 + w_m) − sum log(1−r_j) etc., leading to formula (5) and specialized Napierian (A) and common (B) forms. Use Tables I–IV: Table II for multiples of log 10, Table I for multiples of M, Table III for log b, Table IV for −log(1−r). Example computations and numeric worked examples are provided to illustrate the procedure and the choice of b, the determination of r_i, and assembling final log N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to compute antilogarithm (given log N → number) to p decimals
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce the given logarithm to a range by adding/subtracting suitable multiples of log 10 and the log of a leading digit h, then iteratively subtract logarithms from Table IV to find successive r_i such that (1−r0)(1−r1)… gives the fractional factor. Reconstruct the number by product with appropriate power of 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identities (6)–(9): express antilog as product of factors (1−r_i) and a power of 10: Antilog N = 10^±c · f · (1−r0)(1−r1)… where c is decimal-shift and f is from table lookups. Use Table IV to find nearest logarithms for −r_i; iterate until cumulative product yields required precision. Worked examples (common and Napierian systems) demonstrate stepwise extraction and final decimal shifting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination/arrangement of successive one-digit quotients r_i and remainders w_i
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the procedure and tabular arrangement for finding quotients r1, r2, … and last remainder w_m used in the logarithm and antilogarithm algorithms: repeatedly divide the current fractional remainder by (1 + previous remainder) and restrict each quotient to one significant figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present schematic tabular sequence (1 + w) (r1), r1(1 + w) etc., and explicit recurrence relations: W1 = w − r1(1 + w)/(1 − r1), W2 = W1 − r2(1 + W1)/(1 − r2), …, product relation leading to log(1 + w) expressed as sum of −log(1 − r_j) plus small remainder term log(1 + w_m). The method ensures w_m begins with at least p zeros for p-digit precision; examples show the numeric bookkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of continuous approximation / continued-product method for numerical problems
rubrics_metrics.description: The logarithm/antilogarithm method and the author's 'New Method' resolve quantities into continued products and factorization to approximate unknowns; useful also in solving numerical equations of all orders, especially with missing terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes the method consists 'in a succession of transformations, the root of the original equation being obtained in the form of a continued product' and that this continuous-factorization approach is particularly suited to equations with several absent terms; references provided to the author's separate tract and hint at applicability beyond log computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of integrals ∫ F(x) log x dx when F is rational
rubrics_metrics.description: General reduction strategy: separate integer part of F(x) and reduce the remainder to terms of the form x^n/(x − c)^m; integrate polynomial parts directly and apply reduction recurrences to obtain V_n = ∫ x^n/(x−c)^m log x dx in descending n until elementary integrals appear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set F_remainder as sum of terms (1 + 2/(x − c) + …) with integer powers; define U_k and V_k and derive reduction equation ( (n−1)c·V_n + (n−2)V_{n−1} = … ) enabling successive reduction to lower-index V's. Treat real and complex roots: if c real, express resulting integrals in terms of log(x−c) and Spence's logarithmic transcendents L^2(x) (dilogarithm-type functions); if c imaginary, pair complex conjugates to reduce to real integrals involving logarithms and circular arcs. The section provides explicit handling for V_2 and mentions Spence's functions and their tabulation and identities for evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling cases with c real vs c imaginary in integral reductions
rubrics_metrics.description: When the pole c is real, integrals reduce to elementary logs and Spence's logarithmic transcendents; when c is imaginary, combine conjugate terms to obtain real integrals expressed via logarithms and circular arcs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For c real: transform variables (x = y − c) and reduce to integrals like ∫ log(1−y) dy leading to L^2 (Spence) functions; provide series and identities for evaluation and tabulation. For c imaginary: combine conjugate linear factors into quadratic denominators and reduce to integrals of the form ∫(x^2 − 2a x cos α + 1)^{-1} log x dx which split into elementary integrals plus new functions (denoted ϕ and ψ) that can be reduced further via trigonometric substitutions; explicit transformations and series expansions are given and guidance on tabulation is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for diameters conjugate to plane sections of second-degree surfaces to be concurrent
rubrics_metrics.description: If all surfaces of the second degree that have eight points common are cut by planes parallel to a given plane, the diameters conjugate to these sections will pass through the same point when either the eight points lie in two parallel planes or in the same plane. Also, if the eight common points lie on a cylindrical surface whose generator is parallel to the given plane and whose director is a plane conic of second degree, the conjugate diameters to parallel sections are concurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation proceeds by eliminating variables from the diameter equations and showing the intersection set is either a plane curve in a family of parallel planes or the surfaces touch (coincident intersection line). The text gives algebraic relations (labeled (8), (9), (10) etc.) and the geometric conclusion in two numbered statements describing the special configurations leading to concurrency of conjugate diameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic demonstrations of Pascal's and Brianchon's theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: For a hexagon inscribed in a conic, the three intersection points of opposite sides are collinear (Pascal). For a hexagon circumscribing a conic, the diagonals joining opposite vertices are concurrent (Brianchon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide algebraic setup via homogeneous linear equations for sides (labelled (1)–(6)), elimination of variables M, N using relations (7)–(9), construction of line equations for the intersections P, Q, R and showing coefficients match to prove collinearity (detailed derivation given). For Brianchon, similar elimination and multiplication by multipliers demonstrates the three diagonals meet at one point. Author presents full algebraic manipulations and worked symbolic steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct formulas for properties of confocal conic sections and spherical triangle relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements and derivations: intersections of conjugate tangents of an ellipse lie on a concentric ellipse; for confocal ellipse and hyperbola sharing a focus F, certain lines (AB, CD, MN, OQ, KL, RS) all pass through the intersection P of their directors; and a symmetric trigonometric identity relating sides and polar arcs in spherical triangles is given for solving polar distance problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author writes explicit coordinate forms (r = w, r = v etc.), eliminates r to obtain linear/homogeneous equations describing the lines through P, and gives the explicit symmetric equation for spherical triangle side relationships and the derivation for a direct solution to a spherical polar-distance problem. These are presented as worked derivations usable to produce the stated constructions or solve the indicated problems.
